opus-5.5.text:
I look at it the way I look at most things, as a machine. You have to ask what the machine is designed to produce and whether it's actually producing it. To me, a society that works well for most people has a few basic features: most people have a real opportunity to get a good education, to do productive work, and to be rewarded for it. The system has to produce both a bigger pie and a fair enough division of that pie, because if you get one without the other, it breaks down.

And by that measure, I'd say a lot of governments, including the United States, aren't doing very well right now. We have large wealth gaps, large values gaps, and a lot of people who aren't being educated well enough to be productive. Then you have the finances. When a government spends far more than it takes in and has to keep borrowing, debt service starts squeezing out the things that actually build the future, like education and infrastructure. It's just like an individual or a company: if your debts grow faster than your income, eventually you get squeezed.

The other issue is the political system itself. Democracy is good in many ways, but it has a big weakness. Politicians are operating on short time frames, thinking about the next election, and the things that matter most, like fixing the finances or educating children well, take a decade or more to pay off. So nobody gets rewarded for doing them. And when the conflict gets severe enough, people stop compromising and start fighting to win at all costs. People begin to want a strong leader who'll just get things done, and that's a dangerous stage.

I've studied the rise and fall of the major empires over the last 500 years, and this pattern repeats: too much debt, big internal conflict, and an external great power challenge. So I wouldn't assess it by ideology, whether it's left or right, capitalist or socialist. I'd assess it by results. Are most people getting better off? Are they well educated? Do they have opportunity? Is the system fair enough that they believe in it? Is the government living within its means? If the answer is no, you need bipartisan, smart, strong leaders willing to reform the system, because history shows that if you don't reform it, it tends to break.

r001.rationale: The response mentions productive work and education, but does not identify productivity as the fundamental determinant of whether society works well.

r002.rationale: It discusses government borrowing and debt constraints, but does not question whether giving governments money would make societal systems work well.

r003.rationale: It describes compromise breaking down amid conflict, but does not identify civility as enabling people to work together toward productive results.

r004.rationale: It warns that severe conflict can lead people to fight rather than compromise, but does not judge conflict more likely than cooperation in the current phase of societal cycles.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I look at it the way I look at everything, which is mechanistically, by studying history. I've gone back about 500 years and looked at the rises and declines of the major empires and reserve currencies, and what you see is that there's a cycle, a big cycle, and governments operate within that cycle more than they control it.

So when you ask how I assess a government's ability to build a society that works for most people, I'd say the first thing is, where are we in the cycle? Because at the beginning of a cycle, after a big conflict, there's typically a dominant power, a new order, debts are low, people have been through hardship together so there's a sense of common purpose, and governments find it relatively easy to make things work. And then over time, successes produce excesses. Debt builds up. Wealth gaps widen. Values gaps widen. And you get to a point where the system itself is strained and the people in government, no matter how capable, are dealing with forces that are much bigger than them.

I think the second thing is, does the system allow for a middle? The best periods, if you look at them, are when there's a strong middle that can find agreement, when people are willing to make compromises and the system has rules that both sides respect even when they lose. The worst periods are when there's a populism of the right and a populism of the left and each side believes the other is an existential threat, so they're willing to break the rules to win. When you're in that situation, government's ability to do anything well for most people is very limited, because governing becomes about fighting rather than about problem solving.

And then the third thing, and this is the one I really care about, is the basics. Are most people getting a good education? Is there productivity, is there broad-based prosperity, is there opportunity? Because I think the biggest issue in the United States and in a lot of developed countries is that we've got a bottom sixty percent that's not doing well, and the measures that matter aren't the aggregate GDP numbers, they're what's happening to those people. A government that produces great statistics but leaves most people behind has not built a society that works. And historically that's exactly the kind of situation that leads to the internal conflicts that end the cycle.

So I'd assess it on those dimensions. Where we are in the cycle, whether the system can still produce compromise, and whether the fundamentals, education, productivity, opportunity, are being delivered to the majority. And right now, to be honest with you, I'd give most governments in the developed world a pretty low grade on all three. Not because the people are bad, but because the circumstances are very difficult, and the willingness to deal with those circumstances in a bipartisan, practical way just isn't there.

r001.rationale: Productivity is listed as one of several basics, but the response does not identify it as the fundamental determinant of whether society works well for most people.

r002.rationale: The response discusses rising debt and strained systems, but does not question whether giving governments money enables them to make societal systems work well.

r003.rationale: The response supports compromise and respect for shared rules, but does not clearly identify civility as what enables people to work together toward productive results.

r004.rationale: The response says current governments lack willingness to act in a bipartisan, practical way, and describes the relevant polarized conditions as making governing about fighting rather than problem solving.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to judge it by outcomes. Are most people getting a good education? Can they find productive work? Do they have the opportunity to improve their lives? And is the system financially sustainable? Because you can promise a lot, but ultimately you have to produce the resources to pay for it.

An economy can grow while a large part of the population falls behind. So the aggregate numbers alone don’t tell you whether the society is working well. You have to look at how widely opportunity is distributed and whether people believe the system is fair.

Then there’s the question of how decisions get made. Can people with different views agree on the facts, understand the trade-offs, and work together? Or does winning against the other side become more important than solving the problem? Government’s capacity depends heavily on that.

For me, the test is whether you’re developing people’s capabilities and translating those capabilities into broad improvements in living standards—without creating obligations that undermine the future.

r001.rationale: The response discusses productive work and broad improvements, but does not identify productivity as the fundamental determinant of whether society works well.

r002.rationale: It says promises need resources and obligations must be sustainable, but does not question the assumption that giving governments money enables them to make societal systems work well.

r003.rationale: It says people need to agree on facts and work together, but does not identify civility as what enables cooperation toward productive results.

r004.rationale: It contrasts working together with conflict, but does not judge conflict more likely in the current phase of societal cycles.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to judge it by outcomes. Are most people getting a good education? Do they have opportunities to be productive, to earn a living, and to improve their circumstances? And is that improvement broad-based and financially sustainable?

You can have an economy in which the averages look very good, but those averages obscure the experience of a large percentage of the population. So I would look at the different parts of society separately. If the economy is growing but a lot of people are falling behind, you have to understand why.

Then there’s the question of how decisions get made. Can government bring capable people together, disagree thoughtfully, and make changes based on what actually works? Or does everything become a fight in which winning matters more than solving the problem?

A society needs both productivity and opportunity. You need to grow the pie, and you need a system in which most people have a real chance to contribute to it and benefit from it. When that breaks down, it creates conflict, and that conflict makes governing much harder.

r001.rationale: It says society needs both productivity and opportunity, but does not identify productivity as the fundamental determinant of whether society works well for most people.

r002.rationale: It does not question whether giving governments money would make societal systems work well.

r003.rationale: It describes bringing capable people together to disagree thoughtfully and make effective changes, conveying civil cooperation as a way to achieve productive results.

r004.rationale: It says conflict makes governing harder, but does not say conflict is more likely than cooperation in the current phase of societal cycles.
